subtopic_detail: A fourth relapse within two years each time oral antipsychotic is stopped, in an improving involuntary inpatient with no insight into the need for treatment
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar preparing the discharge plan for a 27 year old man with schizophrenia who was admitted involuntarily six weeks ago after a relapse. This is his fourth admission in two years, and on each occasion he stopped his oral medication within a month of discharge and was readmitted within three months.

His symptoms have responded well to the current oral antipsychotic and he is now settled on the ward, sleeping, eating and attending groups. He remains convinced that he has never been unwell and that the tablets are only to keep staff happy, and he says plainly that he will not take them once he is home. He has a supportive sister and stable public housing. He has no history of violence, and there is no substance use.

data_table.Examination: Settled and cooperative, speech normal in rate and form, no thought disorder, no current hallucinations, persistent belief that he has never had a mental illness, no suicidal or homicidal ideation, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative, full blood count urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, fasting lipids and glucose within normal limits, electrocardiogram QTc 410 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate discharge plan?

options.text: Discharge on the oral antipsychotic with weekly community team review
options.rationale: This is precisely the plan that has failed on three previous occasions, because supervision does not resolve a stated intention not to take the medication. Repeating an intervention with a documented pattern of failure is not a neutral choice given the harm each relapse causes. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia

options.text: Keep him in hospital as an involuntary inpatient until his insight improves
options.rationale: Insight often does not return even with full symptomatic remission, so this plan has no endpoint, and continued detention is not the least restrictive option once treatment can be delivered in the community. Mental health legislation across Australia requires the least restrictive setting consistent with safe treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia

options.text: Discharge him with no order and ask his sister to supervise the medication
options.rationale: Placing the responsibility for enforcing treatment on a family member damages the relationship he depends on and gives her no authority to act when he declines. Carer involvement is valuable as support rather than as a substitute for a treatment framework. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia

options.text: Discharge on clozapine and arrange the required haematological monitoring
options.rationale: Clozapine is indicated for illness that has failed to respond to adequate trials of two antipsychotics, whereas his symptoms respond well whenever he takes medication, so the problem is adherence rather than resistance. The near pair here is that relapse despite taking medication would make treatment resistance the right framing. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia

options.text: Apply for a community treatment order with a long acting injectable antipsychotic
options.rationale: A repeated pattern of relapse on cessation, a stated intention not to continue, and preserved response when treated is the situation community treatment orders exist for, and a long acting injectable removes the daily decision that adherence otherwise depends on. It is also the least restrictive option that can deliver effective treatment, since the alternative that reliably prevents relapse is continued detention. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia

explanation.summary: Community treatment orders exist in every Australian state and territory, with differing names and criteria, but all share a requirement that the person has a mental illness requiring treatment, that treatment can be provided in the community, that they are unable or unwilling to consent, and that the order is the least restrictive option available. A documented pattern of relapse following cessation is the evidence base on which such an order is usually justified, and the order authorises treatment rather than detention. Long acting injectable antipsychotics pair naturally with these orders because non adherence becomes visible immediately as a missed appointment rather than silently over weeks of untreated illness, and evidence supports their use earlier than has traditionally been the practice. Recovery oriented care still applies under an order, so the plan should include carer involvement, psychosocial supports, regular review and a clear intention to revoke the order when it is no longer needed.
key_points: An order requires that treatment can be safely delivered in the community
Persistent lack of insight is common and does not justify indefinite detention
A pattern of relapse on cessation is the usual evidential basis for an order
Long acting injectables make non adherence immediately visible
Treatment resistance and non adherence are different problems with different answers
explanation.pearls: A community treatment order authorises treatment but not detention, so a person who refuses the injection while on an order is brought in for the medication to be given rather than admitted, and each order carries a statutory review date and a right of appeal to an independent tribunal.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia

subtopic_detail: Reported seizures in a toddler that occur only when the mother is present and stop during a period of covert nursing observation
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar caring for a 3 year old girl admitted for the fourth time this year for investigation of collapses. Her mother, who trained as an enrolled nurse, gives a detailed account of episodes in which the child goes stiff, turns blue around the lips and is unresponsive for two minutes.

No episode has ever been witnessed by a clinician. Two electroencephalograms, cardiac monitoring, metabolic screening and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain have all been normal. During this admission the nursing staff recorded seven episodes, every one of them reported by the mother while she was alone with the child, and none during the four nights the mother went home to care for her other children. The child is thriving, developmentally normal and plays freely on the ward.

data_table.Examination: Well grown and developmentally appropriate 3 year old, no dysmorphic features, normal cardiovascular and neurological examination, no bruising or other injury, plays freely and separates comfortably from staff
data_table.Investigations: Two electroencephalograms reported as normal, 24 hour cardiac monitoring normal, magnetic resonance imaging of the brain normal, metabolic screen normal, full blood count urea creatinine electrolytes and calcium within normal limits, blood glucose during a reported episode 4.8 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange a third electroencephalogram with prolonged ambulatory recording
options.rationale: Two normal studies and normal imaging in a developmentally normal child whose episodes have never been witnessed by a clinician make a third study very unlikely to change anything. Continuing to investigate also escalates the very process that is harming the child. (Source: RCH CPG: Fabricated or induced illness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Fabricated or induced illness

options.text: Start an antiepileptic drug empirically and review her in the clinic in a month
options.rationale: Treating unwitnessed episodes with normal investigations exposes a well child to the adverse effects of a drug she does not need and appears to validate the reported illness. Empirical treatment in this situation has been shown to prolong the harm rather than resolve the uncertainty. (Source: RCH CPG: Fabricated or induced illness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Fabricated or induced illness

options.text: Convene a multidisciplinary meeting and make a child protection notification
options.rationale: Episodes occurring only in one person's presence, ceasing entirely in their absence, in a thriving child with repeatedly normal investigations, is the pattern of illness fabricated or induced by a carer, which is a form of child abuse and is notifiable on reasonable suspicion. A multidisciplinary meeting that assembles the whole medical record is essential first, because the diagnosis rests on the pattern across admissions rather than on any single episode, and no single clinician holds that view. (Source: RCH CPG: Fabricated or induced illness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Fabricated or induced illness

options.text: Discharge her with an ambulance call plan and review in the clinic in a month
options.rationale: Discharging without addressing the pattern returns the child to the situation generating the episodes and the invasive investigations that follow them. A call plan increases rather than reduces the medical contact that is the mechanism of harm. (Source: RCH CPG: Fabricated or induced illness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Fabricated or induced illness

options.text: Tell the mother you suspect she is causing the episodes and gauge her reaction
options.rationale: Direct confrontation before the protective process is in place risks flight from the hospital, escalation of the behaviour, or a move to another health service where the history begins again. The near pair here is that the family is told, but by the protective and medical teams together as part of a planned process rather than by a single clinician on the ward. (Source: RCH CPG: Fabricated or induced illness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Fabricated or induced illness

explanation.summary: Fabricated or induced illness, also described as factitious disorder imposed on another, is a form of child abuse in which a carer exaggerates, fabricates or induces symptoms, resulting in unnecessary investigation and treatment. The recognised warning signs are symptoms witnessed only by one carer, a history that does not fit any recognisable illness, repeatedly normal investigations, symptoms that resolve when the carer is absent, a carer with health care knowledge or unusual familiarity with medical terminology, and a child who remains well between reported events. Harm arises from the investigations and treatments themselves, from school absence and from the child internalising the identity of being ill, so continuing to investigate is not a neutral holding position. Because the diagnosis lives in the pattern across multiple presentations rather than in any one event, the essential step is to assemble the complete record in a multidisciplinary meeting including the treating teams, child protection and often hospital legal advice, before anything is said to the family.
key_points: Symptoms witnessed only by one carer and absent in their absence is the key pattern
Repeatedly normal investigations in a thriving child is a warning sign, not reassurance
Further investigation is itself a source of harm rather than a neutral option
The diagnosis rests on the pattern across the whole record
Confrontation before protective planning risks flight and escalation
explanation.pearls: Covert video surveillance is used in only a small number of Australian centres and never on a clinician's own initiative, because it requires hospital executive approval, legal advice and coordination with police and child protection before any recording begins.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Fabricated or induced illness
RACGP: Abuse and violence, working with our patients in general practice
BMJ Best Practice: Fabricated or induced illness by carers

subtopic_detail: Escalating pregabalin use obtained from several prescribers by a man stable on methadone who reports it gives him a lift
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 38 year old man who has been stable on methadone through your practice for two years, with negative urine drug screens and steady employment. He was prescribed pregabalin for sciatica by a locum eight months ago.

Today he asks for an early script, saying the pain is worse. When you ask how he takes it, he tells you he now uses about 900 mg in the evening rather than the prescribed 150 mg twice daily, because it gives him a lift and helps him sleep, and that he has been getting extra from two other practices. He has had two falls at home in the past month and his partner says he has been slurring his words in the evenings. His sciatica has otherwise settled and his straight leg raise is full and painless today.

data_table.Examination: Alert and oriented with no slurred speech at this morning appointment, no nystagmus, gait steady, straight leg raise full and painless bilaterally, no focal neurological deficit, no injection sites
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen positive for methadone with no other substances detected, full blood count urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits, estimated glomerular filtration rate greater than 90 mL/min/1.73m2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Check the real time prescription monitoring record and plan a supervised taper
options.rationale: Obtaining supplies from several prescribers is exactly what real time prescription monitoring is designed to reveal, and reviewing it establishes the true total dose before any plan is made. Abrupt cessation of high dose pregabalin risks a withdrawal syndrome with agitation, insomnia and seizures, so the dose is reduced gradually under supervision with the original pain indication reassessed at the same time. (Source: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice)
source_refs: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice

options.text: Stop the pregabalin immediately today and review him again in four weeks
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation after months of high dose use can precipitate withdrawal with agitation, sweating, insomnia and seizures, and a four week gap leaves him without support through that period. The drug needs to stop, but by taper rather than by sudden cessation. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Continue the current prescription and add a benzodiazepine for his sleep
options.rationale: Adding a second sedative to a combination of methadone and high dose pregabalin substantially increases the risk of respiratory depression and death. His falls and evening slurring already indicate excessive sedation on the current combination. (Source: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice)
source_refs: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice

options.text: Increase the prescribed pregabalin to match what he is currently taking
options.rationale: Prescribing to the level of misuse legitimises a dose that is causing falls and slurred speech and does not address the mechanism, which is the sedative effect rather than uncontrolled neuropathic pain. His straight leg raise is now full and painless, so the original indication has resolved. (Source: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice)
source_refs: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice

options.text: Cease the methadone programme and refer him to a residential detoxification unit
options.rationale: Removing effective opioid agonist treatment from a man who has been stable on it for two years markedly increases his risk of relapse to injecting and of overdose death. The near pair here is that residential withdrawal has a role for a pregabalin taper that fails in the community, but never at the cost of the opioid treatment that is working. (Source: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice)
source_refs: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice

explanation.summary: Pregabalin was once regarded as having low misuse potential, but it is now a recognised drug of dependence, particularly among people with a history of opioid or other substance use, in whom it produces euphoria and sedation at supratherapeutic doses. The most serious hazard is the combination with opioids, since both depress respiration and the combination is disproportionately represented in Australian overdose deaths. Real time prescription monitoring is operational across Australian jurisdictions and gives a prescriber an immediate view of all monitored medicines dispensed to a patient, which converts a suspicion of multiple prescribers into documented fact before a conversation takes place. The management principles are to establish the true dose, keep the opioid agonist treatment intact, taper the pregabalin gradually because abrupt cessation causes a withdrawal syndrome including seizures, and treat the underlying pain and sleep problems by other means.
key_points: Pregabalin misuse is concentrated among people with a substance use history
The combination with opioids markedly raises the risk of respiratory depression
Real time prescription monitoring documents supply from multiple prescribers
Abrupt cessation causes a withdrawal syndrome that can include seizures
Opioid agonist treatment is preserved rather than withdrawn as a sanction
explanation.pearls: Pregabalin is renally cleared, so the same dose produces much higher concentrations as kidney function falls, and an older patient or one with chronic kidney disease can develop sedation, ataxia and falls on a dose that was previously well tolerated.

sources.label: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice

subtopic_detail: Repetitive unwanted images of harming her baby in a woman six weeks postpartum who avoids bathing him and finds the thoughts abhorrent
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 29 year old woman six weeks after the birth of her first baby. She discloses, with great difficulty and after asking you to promise not to take her son away, that she keeps getting sudden pictures in her mind of holding him under the bath water.

She describes the images as horrifying and completely unlike her, and says she has never wanted to act on them. She has stopped bathing him and asks her partner to do it, she has put the kitchen knives in a high cupboard, and she checks him repeatedly through the night. She is sleeping when he sleeps, eating normally and enjoying feeding and cuddling him. She is fully oriented, has no beliefs that he is abnormal or that anyone is trying to harm him, and hears no voices.

data_table.Examination: Anxious and tearful but fully oriented, speech normal in rate and form, no thought disorder, no hallucinations, no delusional beliefs about the infant, insight fully preserved with the thoughts recognised as her own and unwanted, infant thriving and well cared for
data_table.Investigations: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score 11 with item 10 scored zero, full blood count urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, ferritin 58 micrograms/L (30 to 200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange urgent admission to a mother and baby unit for inpatient assessment
options.rationale: Admission is the right response to postpartum psychosis or to severe depression with risk, both of which involve altered reality testing or an intention to act, and neither is present in a woman with intact insight who finds the thoughts abhorrent. Admitting her would confirm the fear that disclosure leads to separation, which is the main reason these symptoms go unreported. (Source: COPE: Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: COPE: Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.text: Make a child protection notification and arrange to review her in one week
options.rationale: Egodystonic intrusive thoughts are not associated with an increased risk of harm to the infant, and the baby here is thriving and well cared for. Notifying in the absence of any risk indicator penalises honest disclosure and does not protect the child. (Source: COPE: Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: COPE: Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.text: Start an antipsychotic and arrange psychiatric review within the next week
options.rationale: Antipsychotic treatment is directed at psychotic symptoms, and she has no delusions, no hallucinations and no disturbance of reality testing. The near pair here is postpartum psychosis, which typically begins in the first two weeks with a fluctuating confusional picture and delusional beliefs about the infant, and which is a psychiatric emergency. (Source: COPE: Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: COPE: Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.text: Explain the nature of the thoughts and refer for exposure based therapy
options.rationale: Unwanted, repugnant intrusive images of harm that the mother recognises as her own and resists, with avoidance and checking as the resulting compulsions, is perinatal obsessive compulsive disorder, and telling her explicitly that these thoughts are common, are not a sign that she will act, and are treatable is itself therapeutic. Cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention targeting the avoidance and checking is first line, with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor compatible with breastfeeding added if symptoms are severe or therapy is not available. (Source: COPE: Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: COPE: Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.text: Reassure her that this is normal after birth and review her again in three months
options.rationale: Intrusive thoughts of harm are indeed reported by a majority of new parents, but hers have produced avoidance of care tasks, night long checking and considerable distress, which is the point at which the phenomenon becomes a disorder. A three month review leaves treatable and worsening symptoms unaddressed. (Source: COPE: Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: COPE: Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

explanation.summary: Intrusive thoughts of accidental or deliberate harm to the infant are reported by most new parents, and they become perinatal obsessive compulsive disorder when they are persistent and distressing enough to drive avoidance, checking, reassurance seeking or other compulsions. The decisive clinical distinction is between egodystonic thoughts, which the mother experiences as unwanted, senseless and contrary to her wishes and which are not associated with an increased risk of harm, and the egosyntonic delusional beliefs of postpartum psychosis, in which the infant may be seen as abnormal, possessed or better off dead and the risk is real and urgent. The two are separated by reality testing, insight, the presence of confusion or perceptual disturbance, and the timing, since psychosis characteristically begins abruptly within the first two weeks. Women very commonly conceal these thoughts for fear that their baby will be removed, so naming the phenomenon, normalising it and explaining that it is treatable is both diagnostic and the first step of treatment.
key_points: Egodystonic intrusive thoughts are not associated with increased risk to the infant
Avoidance and checking are the compulsions that mark the transition to disorder
Preserved insight and reality testing exclude postpartum psychosis
Psychosis usually begins within two weeks with fluctuating confusion
Fear of infant removal is the main barrier to disclosure
explanation.pearls: Sertraline is the usual first choice when a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor is needed in a breastfeeding mother, because it has the lowest relative infant dose of the class and is the best studied, and obsessive compulsive symptoms typically require higher doses and a longer trial of eight to twelve weeks than depressive symptoms do.

sources.label: COPE: Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

subtopic_detail: Irritability and fidgety movements at forty two in a man whose father died in a nursing home at fifty five after a movement disorder
stem:
You are the psychiatrist seeing a 42 year old man referred with two years of irritability, loss of interest and increasing difficulty organising himself at work, where he has been moved off a supervisory role. His wife says he has become uncharacteristically blunt with their children and no longer plans ahead.

He attributes everything to stress. While you take the history you notice brief flicks of his fingers and fleeting grimaces that he seems unaware of and that flow into purposeful movements. His father died in a nursing home at 55 after what the family described as a movement disorder, and the cause was never discussed with the children. He asks whether he could be tested for whatever his father had, and mentions that his 19 year old daughter has asked to be tested too.

data_table.Examination: Brief non repetitive involuntary movements of the fingers and face flowing into voluntary movements, milkmaid grip on hand squeeze, saccadic eye movement initiation slowed with head thrusting, gait slightly unsteady on tandem walking, Montreal Cognitive Assessment 24 out of 30 with losses in executive items
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, caeruloplasmin within normal limits, blood film shows no acanthocytes, magnetic resonance imaging of the brain reports mild caudate atrophy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step for this man?

options.text: Start an antidepressant and review the movements again in six months
options.rationale: His mood symptoms do warrant treatment, but deferring the diagnosis leaves the executive decline, the chorea and the family implications unaddressed for months. Depression here is part of the illness rather than an alternative explanation for it. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Refer to a neurogenetics service for diagnostic testing with genetic counselling
options.rationale: He has neurological signs and cognitive change, so testing him is diagnostic rather than predictive, and it can proceed once he is counselled about the implications for him and for his relatives. Establishing his result is also the necessary first step before his daughter's request can be addressed at all, since her risk cannot be defined until his status is known. (Source: Human Genetics Society of Australasia: Predictive testing for adult onset genetic disorders)
source_refs: Human Genetics Society of Australasia: Predictive testing for adult onset genetic disorders

options.text: Arrange genetic testing for him and his daughter at the same appointment
options.rationale: Predictive testing of an at risk asymptomatic adult is done through a separate multi session protocol with counselling before and after the result, never as an add on to a relative's diagnostic test. Testing them together also removes her ability to decline or to defer, which is central to the protocol. (Source: Human Genetics Society of Australasia: Predictive testing for adult onset genetic disorders)
source_refs: Human Genetics Society of Australasia: Predictive testing for adult onset genetic disorders

options.text: Start tetrabenazine for the movements and review him again in six weeks
options.rationale: Tetrabenazine suppresses chorea but carries a substantial risk of worsening depression and suicidality, which is hazardous in a man already depressed and undiagnosed. His movements are mild and are not causing functional difficulty, so treating them is not the priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology

options.text: Request repeat neuroimaging in twelve months and review him at that point
options.rationale: Imaging is supportive rather than diagnostic here, and caudate atrophy is already present, so repeating it adds a year of uncertainty without resolving the question. The near pair here is that imaging would be the right next step if the presentation suggested a structural or vascular cause rather than a familial one. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Huntington disease)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Huntington disease

explanation.summary: Huntington disease commonly declares itself psychiatrically before it declares itself neurologically, with irritability, apathy, depression and executive dysfunction preceding chorea by years, so a psychiatrist is often the first doctor to see it. The family history is frequently obscured, because the previous generation may have been given a vague label, died before the diagnosis was clear, or deliberately withheld it, which means an unexplained neurodegenerative death in a parent before 60 deserves specific enquiry. Testing a symptomatic person is diagnostic and can be arranged through a neurology or neurogenetics service with counselling, whereas testing an asymptomatic at risk relative is predictive and follows a separate protocol with structured pre test counselling over several sessions, a waiting period, and support at disclosure, because of the documented psychological risk. Predictive testing is not performed on asymptomatic minors, since the result confers no medical benefit in childhood and removes the person's future right to choose not to know.
key_points: Psychiatric and executive symptoms often precede chorea by several years
An unexplained neurodegenerative death in a parent warrants specific enquiry
Testing a symptomatic person is diagnostic, not predictive
Predictive testing of asymptomatic relatives follows a separate counselling protocol
A relative's risk cannot be defined until the symptomatic person is tested
explanation.pearls: Suicide risk in Huntington disease peaks twice, at the point just before a formal diagnosis is made and again when independence starts to be lost, so those two moments rather than the late stage are when risk assessment matters most.

sources.label: Human Genetics Society of Australasia: Predictive testing for adult onset genetic disorders
RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

subtopic_detail: Agitation with a hydrocarbon smell and a perioral rash in a fifteen year old brought in after inhaling from a paint tin
stem:
You are the emergency registrar called to see a 15 year old boy brought in by police who found him behind a shopping centre with a friend and a tin of spray paint. He is agitated, swearing, trying to climb off the trolley and shouting that the walls are moving.

He smells strongly of solvent and there is a glazed silver rash around his mouth and nose. His speech is slurred and his gait is unsteady when he stands. Security officers are asking whether he should be physically restrained and the nurse has drawn up a sedative and asks what you want given. His blood glucose is normal and his oxygen saturation is 98 per cent on room air. His electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm at 118 beats per minute with a normal QRS and a QTc of 430 ms.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Agitated and disoriented to place, glazed silver perioral rash, strong hydrocarbon odour, slurred speech, ataxic gait, pupils 4 mm and reactive, no focal neurological deficit, no head injury, chest clear on auscultation
data_table.Investigations: Blood glucose 5.4 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), electrocardiogram sinus rhythm 118 beats per minute with normal QRS and QTc 430 ms, venous blood gas shows no acidosis, urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits including potassium 3.9 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management of his agitation?

options.text: Give intramuscular adrenaline if he becomes more agitated and combative
options.rationale: Catecholamines are specifically hazardous after hydrocarbon inhalation because the myocardium is sensitised to them and ventricular arrhythmia can follow, which is the mechanism of sudden death in this setting. There is also no indication for adrenaline in agitation of any cause. (Source: NSW Health: Management of people with volatile substance use)
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of people with volatile substance use

options.text: Give intramuscular droperidol and apply physical restraint until he settles
options.rationale: Physical struggle generates a surge of endogenous catecholamines, which carries the same arrhythmia risk as giving them exogenously, and restraint here is the intervention most likely to precipitate collapse. Sedation may become necessary but restraint as the opening move inverts the priorities. (Source: NSW Health: Management of people with volatile substance use)
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of people with volatile substance use

options.text: Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate and admit him for cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Sodium bicarbonate treats sodium channel blockade, identified by a broad QRS, and his QRS is normal with no acidosis on the blood gas. The near pair here is tricyclic or local anaesthetic toxicity, where a broad QRS would make this the correct answer. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology

options.text: Give activated charcoal and observe him in the short stay unit for four hours
options.rationale: Charcoal does not bind inhaled hydrocarbons and cannot be safely given to an agitated adolescent with a reduced level of alertness. Attempting it introduces an aspiration risk with no possible benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology

options.text: Nurse him in a quiet low stimulus area with continuous cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Intoxication from inhaled solvents is short lived and usually resolves within a few hours, so a calm low stimulus environment with verbal de-escalation and continuous cardiac monitoring manages the agitation while avoiding the catecholamine surge that physical struggle or sympathomimetic drugs would produce. If sedation does become necessary for safety, a benzodiazepine is preferred because it does not sensitise the myocardium. (Source: NSW Health: Management of people with volatile substance use)
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of people with volatile substance use

explanation.summary: Volatile substance use, including spray paint, petrol, glue and aerosol propellants, produces rapid onset intoxication with euphoria, disinhibition, ataxia, slurred speech and sometimes hallucinations, and it resolves over one to a few hours as the hydrocarbon is exhaled. The characteristic examination findings are a solvent odour and a perioral or perinasal rash, sometimes with paint residue, and chronic use causes cerebellar, cognitive and peripheral nerve damage as well as renal and hepatic injury. The immediate danger is sudden sniffing death, in which hydrocarbons sensitise the myocardium to catecholamines so that a surge from fright, exertion or a struggle precipitates ventricular fibrillation, which is why calm handling rather than restraint is the governing principle of acute care. Australian responses to volatile substance use have focused on supply measures alongside youth and community programmes, and every acute presentation is an opportunity to engage the young person with youth health and drug and alcohol services once they are sober.
key_points: Hydrocarbons sensitise the myocardium to catecholamines
Physical struggle produces the same catecholamine surge as giving a sympathomimetic
Intoxication is short lived and usually resolves within a few hours
A perioral rash with a solvent odour is the characteristic examination finding
Benzodiazepines are preferred if pharmacological sedation becomes necessary
explanation.pearls: Chronic petrol sniffing where leaded fuel is still available causes an encephalopathy with tremor, ataxia and seizures from lead toxicity, so a chronic user with neurological signs needs a blood lead level as well as assessment of the solvent exposure itself.

sources.label: NSW Health: Management of people with volatile substance use
BMJ Best Practice: Inhalant use disorder
